extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and presenting secondary considerations (objective indicia) and related evidentiary affidavits/declarations in obviousness, enablement, utility, and prior-art attribution contexts during patent examination and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages Disclosed or Inherent
rubrics_metrics.description: The totality of the record must be considered when determining whether a claimed invention would have been obvious; evidence and arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant is not required to have advantages disclosed in the specification; evidence and arguments proffered during prosecution (e.g., In re Chu) should be considered as part of the totality of the record. Examples/citations: In re Chu (advantages not disclosed in spec but considered), In re Zenitz, Ex parte Sasajima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of Production for Commercial Success
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant asserting commercial success to support nonobviousness bears the burden of proof in establishing commercial success; the PTO relies on applicant to provide hard evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO lacks means to gather such evidence in ex parte prosecution, so applicant must present the factual evidence (In re Huang; In re GPAC; In re Paulsen). Examiner may expect documentary evidence of sales, market data, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus Requirement Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Nexus designates a factually and legally sufficient connection between the evidence of commercial success and the claimed invention so that the evidence is of probative value in the nonobviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of nexus should follow MPEP §§716.01(b) and 2145 and case law (Demaco). Applicant must show that the claimed features are responsible for success; mere embodiment of invention in a commercially successful article is insufficient without nexus evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial Success Abroad Relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success abroad, as well as in the United States, is relevant in resolving nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Lindemann Maschinenfabrik GMBH v. American Hoist & Derrick Co.; foreign sales/market success can be considered as part of objective evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial Success Must Be Commensurate in Scope With Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness (including commercial success) must be commensurate in scope with the claims; success must be due to claimed features and not unclaimed features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If commercial success relates to narrower features (e.g., dependent claim features) but the asserted claims are broader, the success may not be commensurate and thus not probative (In re Tiffin; Joy Technologies v. Manbeck). See MPEP §§716.01(b) and 2145.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit Language Attributing Success Insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration merely attributing commercial success to a product 'constructed according to the disclosure and claims' does not establish nexus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such generic language does not show the sold product corresponds to the claimed invention or that the success is attributable to the claimed features (Ex parte Standish). More specific corroborating evidence is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof When Claimed Invention Not Coextensive With Commercial Product
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claimed invention is not coextensive with the commercial product/process, applicant must show a legally sufficient relationship between the claimed feature and the commercial product or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant need not show success at every point in a claimed range if persuasive evidence shows typical operation approximates the commercially successful point (In re Hollingsworth; Demaco). Provide affidavits indicating operation across range if relying on a point within range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial Success Must Be Attributable to Claimed Features (Not Extraneous Factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success must result from the invention claimed in a marketplace where consumers choose on objective principles and not from heavy promotion, advertising shifts, brand loyalty, blocking patents, or other extraneous business events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor opinions as to purchaser motivation are insufficient (In re Huang). Consider effects of advertising, market conditions, preexisting market leadership, blocking patents (UCB v. Actavis), licensing programs, etc. Case examples include In re Mageli, In re Noznick, Pentec, EWP Corp., Hybritech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial Success Must Flow From Functions/Advantages Disclosed or Inherent in Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: To be pertinent to nonobviousness, commercial success of devices within the claims must flow from functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification; success should not be due to improvements by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success deriving from a unique combination of unclaimed ingredients or later-modified embodiments may not show nonobviousness of the claimed invention (In re Vamco; Merck & Cie v. Gnosis). Ensure linkage between disclosed/inherent advantages and market success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design Cases: Nexus Especially Difficult
rubrics_metrics.description: In design patent cases, establishing nexus between commercial success and the claimed design is especially difficult; success must be clearly attributable to the design and not to brand recognition or improved performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design success must be shown to arise from the design itself (Litton Systems v. Whirlpool). Be cautious attributing sales to a design when other factors could explain success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales Figures Must Be Adequately Defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross sales figures alone do not show commercial success absent evidence as to market share, the time period of sales, or what sales would normally be expected in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide market share data, time period, baseline expectations, and contextual information (Cable Electric Products v. Genmark; Ex parte Standish). Overreliance on raw gross sales is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-Felt Need — Existence and Characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must satisfy a long-felt need which was recognized, persistent, and not solved by others to be a persuasive secondary consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-felt need requires objective evidence that a recognized problem existed for a long period without solution; if the problem was first recognized by the inventor or already satisfied by prior art, long-felt need is absent (In re Gershon; Newell Companies v. Kenney). The invention must actually satisfy the need (In re Cavanagh).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-Felt Need Measured From Date Problem Identified
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-felt need is analyzed as of the date the problem is identified and efforts are made to solve it, not as of the date of the most pertinent prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure from the time the problem was identified and attempts to solve it occurred (Texas Instruments v. ITC). Use contemporaneous documentation of problem recognition and efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Other Factors for Long-Felt Need
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure of others to solve a problem may be due to lack of interest or appreciation of marketability rather than lack of technical know-how; these factors must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative/regulatory context or market disinterest can explain lack of solutions and may weaken or support a long-felt need inference (Scully Signal; Environmental Designs v. Union Oil). Affidavits by bona fide licensees may add weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of Experts as Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of disbelief or skepticism by experts prior to the invention constitute strong evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-invention expert incredulity and prolonged research efforts can rebut prima facie obviousness (United States v. Adams; In re Dow Chemical; Burlington Industries v. Quigg). Testimony of expert skepticism should be weighed as objective indicia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying by Competitors as Secondary Consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that competitors copied the invention (rather than used prior art) may be a relevant secondary consideration supporting nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying requires proof of efforts to replicate a specific product (internal documents, disassembly, photos used as blueprint) or access to confidential disclosures (Iron Grip; Wyers v. Master Lock; Liqwd v. L’Oreal). Copying is persuasive where substantial design effort failed and competitor then copied (Dow Chemical; Panduit), but mere copying is not dispositive—copying may be for reasons unrelated to patentability (Cable Electric; Pentec). Copies that are not substantially similar or where little effort was expended are not persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperability of References — Presumption of Operability
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent is presumed valid, and that presumption includes operability; examiners should not express opinions on operability of a patent reference and affidavits attacking operability must rebut the presumption by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits/declarations must provide sufficient proof; failures of experimenters uninterested in succeeding are entitled to little weight (In re Sasse; Metropolitan Eng. Co. v. Coe; In re Weber; In re Michalek; In re Reid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Alleged Inoperability on Reference Effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: If an affidavit asserts inoperability only for features not relied upon, the reference remains effective for its operative features. If a reference is alleged inoperative, applicant's claims must distinguish from that alleged inoperative disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re Shepherd; In re Crosby; In re Epstein. Show that relied-upon features are operative or distinguish claims from the inoperative disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility/Enablement Burden-Shifting and Affidavit Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Once examiner establishes a prima facie lack of enablement, applicant must present persuasive arguments, supported by suitable proofs where necessary, that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention from the disclosure; affidavits/declarations cannot establish facts the specification should have recited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits offering expert construction of non-described elements are generally insufficient (In re Brandstadter; In re Howarth; In re Buchner). Affidavits purporting only to explain or interpret a disclosure are usually not considered unless they explain underlying factual bases and are evaluated case-by-case (In re Oppenauer; Glaser v. Strickland). See MPEP §§2164-2164.08(c), 2107.02, 2107-2107.03 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution Affidavit/Declaration Requirements to Overcome Pre-AIA 102 Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain circumstances, an affidavit or declaration may be submitted to attribute a disclosure in a reference to the inventor (or joint inventor) to overcome a rejection based on pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102; such submissions are governed by 37 CFR 1.132 (and 1.130/1.131 distinctions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unequivocal declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 that inventor S conceived the subject matter can overcome the rejection if corroborated (In re DeBaun). The declaration must explain presence of additional inventors in references when necessary, and documentary evidence contradicting inventors' statements may justify maintaining the rejection (In re Katz; In re Carreira; Ex parte Kroger). Affidavits of attribution are treated under 37 CFR 1.132 for pre-AIA cases and under 1.130 for current 35 U.S.C. 102 situations. Examples provided in MPEP and illustrative examples (Example 1/2) show how attribution changes reference status.
